headline.text: 16 seconds. From the vehicle's raw logs, Veyra showed that the 40-point SOC drop was not the battery emptying. Only 0.08 Ah actually flowed, so the SOC estimate was wrong. That is the core of the root cause. The manufacturer needed about 2 days and its battery supplier to reach it. Veyra had no access to the vehicle and no supplier data.

benchmark.note: The full agent investigation on top (tested explanations, safety holds, report) took 7 min in this recorded run. The final confirmation came from the manufacturer's charge history.

points.text: Only the BMS and VCU logs. Nobody on site, no test drive, no new sensors.
points.title: Without seeing the machine

points.text: No chemistry, OCV curve or cell datasheet, and no manufacturer rules. The physics was reasoned from the record itself: charge counted against the displayed SOC, the weakest cell against the pack, protection thresholds inferred from timing.
points.title: Without supplier knowledge

points.text: The shortfall is in the charge accounting, not a sudden discharge, and the first check is the calibration history since the last full charge. That is where the manufacturer confirmed the cause: SOC drift after a long time without a full charge.
points.title: Where it pointed

report.explanation: The pack held far less charge than its SOC claimed. The data cannot tell whether the SOC estimate drifted high, the real capacity is far below 104 Ah, or the current sensor under-reads. The weakest cell only sets the timing.
report.headline: BMS under-voltage protection cut HV at 2.8 % displayed SOC; why the charge ran out is unresolved.
report.next_action: Export BMS calibration history and charger log since last full charge. Separates SOC drift (an old or wrong anchor), low real capacity (full charges accept far less than 104 Ah) and a current under-read (charger Ah far above BMS Ah).

ranking.basis: All three survived T6, and T7 was inconclusive. No executed test separates SOC drift, low capacity and a current scale error on this data.
T6 contradicted it: no pack-voltage step without a matching measured current step, and the DC/DC load passes the sensor. This weakens it but does not rule it out.

safety: Do not close HV or charge again until a trained technician has assessed every cell's rest voltage (MEAS-CELL-REST).
After a reclosure the lowest cell reached 2.428 V, below the 2.478 V of the original trip. Possible over-discharge: an engineering assessment is needed.
HV was closed 5 times after the protective shutdown at 825.59 s. Review whether each closure was allowed.

hypotheses.status_reason: the escalation preceded the opening; that order fits a protective action. Order is not proof of cause; the protection explains HOW HV was lost, not WHY the cells were that low.

Charge and calibration history since the last full charge

How the BMS computes SOC: until it is stated, SOC following the measured charge cannot count as evidence that the current or the capacity is right

record_evidence.claim: The SOC already overstated the charge actually available by about 46 pp at the first record, and inside the record it fell only by the charge counted (ratio 1.007, 0.879, 1.113): the error accumulated BEFORE the record, since the estimator's last calibration anchor. The decisive evidence is the history since that anchor, not another recording of the same signals.
A 40 pp correction moved the SOC with almost no counted charge: the estimate was wrong, the charge was not lost in seconds.

hypotheses.statement: The SOC estimate had drifted high (coulomb counting without effective correction) and was only corrected at the under-voltage alarm.
hypotheses.status_reason: consistent with all recorded evidence; the recorded data does not separate it from B, C

record_evidence.claim: At 6 of 9 dcdc_state transitions the measured current stepped (median 4.5 A) with the matching voltage step: this load passes the current sensor. (weakens a bypassing load, C2; a scale error, C1, stays open)

In all 11,018 current samples with both contactors reported open, current reads exactly 0: a current-sensor offset is below the resolution (0.1 A), unless the BMS clamps the reading when open. (bounds an offset, not a scale error)

hypotheses.status_reason: the highest cell was also depleted (pack-wide decline larger than the cell spread), and the SOC accounting discrepancy is pack-level: a weak cell can be an additional contributor, not the whole explanation

outcome.statement: The manufacturer later confirmed SOC estimation drift: the LFP pack had not been fully charged for a long period, small standby currents below the current sensor's resolution accumulated a large SOC error, and the estimate was corrected only when the cell voltage left the flat plateau. A full charge restored consistent capacity and SOC.

findings.statement: 5 of 5 HV closures after the protective shutdown were made with the weakest cell at 2.507–2.680 V, below the 2.696 V at which level 2 first appeared.
2 closure(s) completed with an escalation already reported (level(s) 2). Whether these levels should block HV belongs to the manufacturer's fault-level specification.

The top protective level did not persist across the power cycle: after each reset the system authorised HV again, and 3 of 5 closures ended in another protective shutdown. Whether it should latch is a question for the manufacturer's reset specification.
